Ok, I read your edited comment.  Looks a lot better know.
One nitpick: I think your set of options needs to grow a lot faster than just superlinearly, I suspect it needs to grew superpolynomially?
However otherwise what you describe is essentially true of all problems in NP, not just the NP hard problems:
Sorting is (trivially) in NP, and you can say that to sort you need to pick one out of n! many permutations (which certainly grows superlinearly and even superpolynomially).
NP hard problems have the distinction that if you solve one of them efficiently, you can solve all of them efficiently, because you can reduce them to each other.  (Basically because NP hard problems allow you to sort-of describe a computer, and reducing them to each other is equivalent to writing an interpreter or compiler.)

text:
There's a lot of nuance in reverse proxies. You're off to a good start with Go as the standard library gives you a very strong and battle-tested HTTP implementation as well as a basic reverse-proxy interface to build with.
Avoiding opening a can of security-issue-worms involves knowing what you're doing and depends heavily on the environment you're operating in. Internally proxying traffic between services? A cakewalk. Translating between HTTP2 or 3 to 1.1? Forwarding origin client IP safely? Sanitizing headers (and I don't mean the in-built sanitization that Go provides)? There's a lot of little things.
Tools like Nginx and Envoy strike from the opposite direction: an extensive suite of configurable tools to reverse proxy the way you need, with relative safety.
Like you, I would almost certainly prefer writing a small reverse proxy in Go over deploying Nginx.
label: analysis
